'''''Celastrus scandens''''', commonly called '''American bittersweet''',<ref>{{cite web |last=Caruso |first=David B. |date=2010-04-03 |title=NYC study: 50 native plants disappearing |publisher=[[PhysOrg.com]] |url=http://www.physorg.com/news189480171.html |access-date=2010-04-03}}</ref> is a [[species]] of [[Celastraceae|bittersweet]] that [[Flower|blooms]] mostly in June and is commonly found on rich, well-drained [[soils]] of [[woodland]]s.

== Description ==
It is a sturdy [[perennial]] [[vine]] that may have twining, woody [[Plant stem|stems]] that are {{convert|30|ft|m}} or longer and {{convert|1|in}} or more thick at the base. The stems are yellowish-green to brown and wind around other [[vegetation]], sometimes killing [[sapling]]s by restricting further growth. It has tiny, scentless [[flowers]] at the tips of the branches. It has colorful, orange [[fruits]] that are the size of a [[pea]]. These fruits are poisonous to humans when ingested, but are favorites of birds.<ref name="MoBot">{{cite web |title=''Celastrus scandens'' |website=Plant Finder |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden |url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=279117 |access-date=2018-07-30}}</ref>

== Uses ==
''C. scandens'' roots were used by [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Native Americans]] and [[American pioneer|pioneers]] to induce [[vomiting]], to treat [[venereal disease]], and to treat [[symptoms]] of [[tuberculosis]].<ref>{{cite book |title=Wildflowers of Iowa Woodlands |url=https://archive.org/details/wildflowersofiow00runk |url-access=registration |first1=Sylvan T. |last1=Runkel |first2=Alvin F. |last2=Bull |year=1979 |publisher=Wallace Homestead Book Co |location=Des Moines, IA |isbn=0-87069-309-3 |page=[https://archive.org/details/wildflowersofiow00runk/page/99 99] |access-date=24 October 2022}}</ref>  It also sees use as a decorative plant, both in landscaping and seasonal floral arrangements.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2006 |title=Plant Guide: American Bittersweet ''Celustus scandens'' L |url=https://plants.sc.egov.usda.gov/DocumentLibrary/plantguide/pdf/pg_cesc.pdf |website=U.S. Department of Agriculture}}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
''Celastrus scandens'' is native to central and eastern North America. It was given the name '''bittersweet''' by colonists in the 18th century because the fruits resembled the appearance of the fruits of common nightshade (''[[Solanum dulcamara]]''), which was also called bittersweet. Today, American bittersweet is the accepted common name of ''C. scandens'' in large part to distinguish it from an invasive relative, ''[[Celastrus orbiculatus|C. orbiculatus]]'' (Oriental bittersweet), from Asia.<ref name="MoBot" /> Hybrids of ''C. orbiculatus'' and ''C. scandens'', entirely produced from ''C. scandens'' seed and ''C. orbicularis'' pollen, showed reduced seed set and small, infertile pollen.<ref>Zaya, D.N., S. A. Leicht-Young, N. B. Pavlovic, K. A. Feldheim and M. V. Ashley. 2015. Genetic characterization of hybridization between native and invasive bittersweet vines (''Celastrus'' spp.). ''Biological Invasions'' 17(10): 2975-2988. {{doi|10.1007/s10530-015-0926-z}}.</ref>
